## Abstract

Modern simulators can generate synthetic camera and LiDAR data with accurate annotations for downstream tasks. In contrast, automotive radar simulation remains less mature because it requires not only a 3D engine to model dynamic objects in the scenes but also electromagnetic material properties, antenna configurations, wave propagation mechanisms, and coherent signal synthesis. Existing frameworks are either proprietary or overly simplified, limiting the scalability of radar raw measurements. This paper presents AuRaSim, a ray-tracing-based automotive frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar simulation framework for dynamic scenarios. Rather than implementing all components from scratch, AuRaSim builds on Blender for efficient dynamic-scene construction and Sionna RT for graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated electromagnetic ray tracing, while introducing radar-specific adaptations for path-resolved propagation with complex coefficients, motion-aware Doppler modeling, and subsequently coherent multi-channel analog-to-digital converter (ADC) cube synthesis based on waveform configurations. Quantitative comparison between simulated and measured range–Doppler maps in digital-twin scenarios achieves a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.147 and a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 16.93 dB, demonstrating the accuracy and fidelity of the synthetic signal. AuRaSim therefore provides a complete and extensible platform for reproducible automotive radar simulation and research. Project homepage: https://wangzhaoze.github.io/aurasim.

## I Introduction

Automotive frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar is a crucial sensing modality for autonomous driving because it provides direct velocity measurements and remains robust under adverse environmental conditions, where camera- and LiDAR-based perception may degrade [1]. However, radar measurements are typically sparse, noisy, affected by the multipath effect, and have limited angular resolution, which challenges conventional signal processing algorithms in complex traffic situations.

Recent deep learning based methods have shown promising performance in overcoming some of these limitations, but their development is still constrained by the lack of large-scale and accurately annotated radar datasets. Compared with camera and LiDAR data, radar raw signals are more challenging to interpret and annotate directly because they require specialized domain knowledge, making high-quality ground-truth acquisition much more expensive. Although several automotive radar datasets have been released in recent years (e.g., [2, 3]), their scale and annotation variety remain more limited than widely used camera- and LiDAR-based benchmarks such as KITTI [4] and nuScenes [5].

Existing approaches to radar data synthesis can broadly be summarized as data-driven and physics-based methods. Data-driven approaches learn the distribution of recorded data and synthesize radar representations using conditional generative models [6, 7]. Such methods can efficiently reproduce measurement statistics and sensor effects that are difficult to formulate analytically. Their applicability is nevertheless often hardware-specific, because the learned distribution is inherently conditioned on the waveform and antenna layout represented during training, such that deviations from these settings can induce domain shifts and degrade generalization to unseen radar hardware. Physics-based simulation instead derives radar measurements from explicit scene, hardware, and propagation models [8]. This enables controlled configuration variation while providing exact scene state as ground truth, making it attractive for radar dataset generation.

However, building a complete automotive radar simulator remains challenging for several reasons. First, realistic driving scenarios require a dynamic 3D scene representation, including environmental geometry, vehicle movements, and articulated or deformable road users. Second, geometrically accurate 3D assets must be assigned electromagnetic material properties for roads, vehicles, buildings, and other traffic participants. Third, relevant electromagnetic propagation mechanisms, including specular and diffuse reflection, diffraction, and multipath propagation, must be modeled to reproduce realistic radar returns, including distributed environmental echoes and multipath-induced ghost targets. Fourth, noise, calibration errors, interference, and other sensor effects remain difficult to reproduce accurately. Finally, resolving these interactions over multiple antenna channels and successive radar frames is computationally expensive. Consequently, automotive radar simulation requires careful trade-offs among physical fidelity, computational efficiency, and practical scenario construction.

Current simulation tools address these challenges to different degrees, with many approaches relying on simplifying assumptions. General-purpose autonomous-driving simulators such as CARLA [9] provide dynamic traffic environments and radar detections but use simplified ray-casting models. Similarly, MATLAB employs a measurement-level probabilistic radar model to generate detections [10]. Commercial radar simulation tools such as Remcom WaveFarer [11], Altair Feko [12] and dSPACE AURELION [13] provide higher-fidelity radar simulation. These platforms demonstrate that physically detailed automotive radar simulation is feasible, but their proprietary and closed-source nature limits wide application within the academic community. This motivates an accessible and extensible framework for flexible research and efficient synthetic-data generation.

In this work, we present AuRaSim, an end-to-end automotive radar simulation framework that addresses this gap by building upon and substantially extending the capabilities of two complementary open-source technologies rather than implementing a complete rendering and propagation stack from scratch. Blender [14] provides a mature solution for constructing complex polygonal scenes, managing reusable 3D assets, i.e., object models and materials, and representing time-varying animations. Sionna RT is an open-source ray tracer originally developed for radio-propagation modeling in communication systems and provides electromagnetic material models and path solvers supporting specular and diffuse reflection, diffraction, and transmission [15]. AuRaSim integrates the complementary capabilities of Blender [14] and Sionna RT [15] and substantially extends them to form an end-to-end automotive FMCW radar simulation framework.

Our main contributions are threefold: (1) We develop a unified scenario-to-signal simulation pipeline that produces path-resolved propagation data, multi-channel analog-to-digital converter (ADC) samples, and derived radar products while preserving a consistent representation of scene state, sensor geometry, and waveform timing. (2) We integrate radar-specific adaptations to the underlying propagation pipeline, including field-of-view-aware ray sampling, propagation-path filtering, and a vertex velocity field that enables Hit-Point Doppler (HPD) modeling for complex dynamic objects. The effectiveness of these components is evaluated through dedicated ablation studies. (3) We establish a digital-twin-based validation workflow by reconstructing representative real-world measurement scenarios with matched 77-GHz radar configurations and quantitatively comparing simulated and measured radar data, including range–Doppler representations, to evaluate the signal fidelity of the proposed simulator.

## II Related Work

### II-A Physics-Based Radar Simulation

Physics-based radar simulation derives sensor measurements from explicit models of scene geometry, electromagnetic propagation, and radar signal formation. Hirsenkorn et al. [16] presented an automotive FMCW radar simulator based on geometrical-optics ray launching, including antenna patterns, reflections, and ray divergence on curved surfaces, comparing range profiles between simulated and measured data. High-fidelity physics-based automotive radar simulation commonly employs the shooting and bouncing rays (SBR) method introduced in [17]. Schüssler et al. [8] extended SBR-based simulation to large multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) arrays and evaluated simulated range-angle spectrum on single-chirp measurements in static scenes and therefore primarily investigated spatial radar responses without Doppler. Mergenthaler et al. [18] later extended this line of work to simulate dynamic pedestrians by incorporating motion-captured animation in a controlled indoor scenario. Thieling et al. [19] proposed a modular architecture that includes physical interactions, scene geometry, object motion, and atmospheric attenuation by rain, with particular emphasis on computational scalability and real-time execution, while detailed implementations of several submodels and quantitative sim-to-real validation are not reported. ViRa [20] follows a different approach by using graphics processing unit (GPU)-based rendering and multi-depth buffers rather than a conventional SBR solver to generate FMCW radar raw data. It supports multi-antenna configurations, configurable beam patterns, and penetration through non-conductive objects, and demonstrates good agreement with measurements. However, its evaluation focuses primarily on indoor robotics scenarios and does not address dynamic automotive traffic scenes or detailed motion-induced Doppler effects. More recently, RadaRays [21] introduced an open-source ray-tracing framework for rotating FMCW radars in mobile robotics. It models reflection, transmission, and material-dependent scattering, outputs range-azimuth responses and provides a substantially more physical alternative to the LiDAR-like ray-casting radar models. However, its output remains at the range-azimuth level rather than providing coherent multi-channel ADC signals, which are required for waveform-level MIMO and Doppler processing. Haider et al. couple CarMaker ray-tracing outputs with an automotive FMCW baseband model including virtual MIMO and sensor impairments [22]. Compared to those existing approaches, AuRaSim provides a unified scenario-to-signal pipeline for dynamic scenes, physics-based propagation, and coherent multi-channel ADC synthesis.

### II-B Generative Radar Synthesis

Data-driven methods typically learn the distribution of a selected radar measurement representation. L2R [23] translates a LiDAR bird’s-eye-view representation into a radar spectrum image using a generative adversarial network (GAN), although phase and channel information absent from the LiDAR input cannot be recovered. Fidelis et al. [24] operate at a lower signal level by generating 16 raw chirps conditioned on motorcycle distance and Gaussian noise, while their evaluation is limited to a single motorcycle moving along a straight trajectory. RF Genesis [25] maps visual scene representations to corresponding mmWave sensing data by using a set of diffusion models to generate large numbers of 3D scenes from application-specific prompts. RadarGen [26], in contrast, generates processed automotive radar point clouds from multi-view imagery together with visual depth, semantic, and motion priors, thereby inheriting errors from the visual cues while not preserving low-level phase or channel information. RadSimReal [27] converts material-assigned reflection points into an intensity radar tensor using a measured point-spread function (PSF) and noise model, but does not generate time-domain ADC data. Xiao et al. [28] learn an attribute-conditioned range–azimuth–Doppler (RAD) tensor from a reflection tensor and waveform-parameter embedding. The resulting output is a real-valued RAD cube rather than a time-domain ADC cube or complex MIMO channel tensor, limiting access to channel-dependent phase information. De Oliveira and Bekooij [6] synthesize short-range FMCW range–Doppler (RD) maps using a bounding-box-conditioned GAN. Wang et al. [7] propose a conditional diffusion model for automotive range–azimuth map generation and subsequently extend it to temporally consistent sequences using a Video Diffusion Transformer [29]. However, these methods learn radar data distributions specific to the sensor configurations represented in datasets, limiting their generalization to customized antenna arrays and waveform parameters. In contrast, AuRaSim supports configurable radar hardware and generates coherent multi-channel ADC signals through physics-based simulation.

### II-C Radar Neural Fields

Neural radar scene representations provide an alternative approach to radar data synthesis by reconstructing a previously observed environment from radar measurements and rendering radar observations from novel sensor views. Radar Fields models frequency-space FMCW measurements using occupancy and view-dependent reflectance fields, but assumes static targets and zero Doppler [30]. DART [31] incorporates range–Doppler measurements and exploits sensor motion to reduce angular ambiguity, but remains limited to static scenes and is sensitive to velocity-estimation error. RF4D [32] represents an outdoor dynamic scene with time-conditioned occupancy and radar cross section (RCS) fields, but its input and output are 2-D range–azimuth scans rather than ADC data. RadarSplat [33] adds Gaussian primitives and models saturation, speckle, and multipath in scanning-radar images. Its current formulation is explicitly restricted to static scenes. RadarSim [34] uses synchronized RGB and single-chip radar recordings to render RD frames from a camera-initialized neural field. These methods synthesize novel views of reconstructed scenes, whereas AuRaSim performs path-resolved simulation of newly constructed dynamic driving scenarios.

### II-D Automotive Radar Simulation Software

Radar simulation tools span a broad range of abstraction levels, from simplified functional models that directly generate detections to physically based simulators that model electromagnetic propagation and raw ADC signals. CARLA [9] employs conical ray casting and directly returns detections characterized by range, angle, and relative velocity, while MATLAB [10] uses statistical measurement-level models based on target signatures and detection probability. Commercial tools provide further high-fidelity capabilities. Ansys HFSS SBR+ [35] supports SBR-based electromagnetic analysis and automotive range–Doppler simulation. Remcom WaveFarer [11] combines ray-based propagation with physical optics (PO) and diffraction models and produces outputs including channel impulse response (CIR) and I/Q data. dSPACE AURELION [13] provides radar-optimized materials, multipath ray tracing, and outputs ranging from CIR and raw radar data to detection and object lists for real-time X-in-the-loop applications. CarMaker Radar RSI [36] integrates physically based radar-environment modeling into dynamic driving scenarios. RadarSimPy [37] combines configurable radar waveforms with point and mesh targets to generate complex baseband samples through ray tracing, while its GPU-accelerated backend is distributed as a precompiled licensed implementation. These tools provide high-fidelity simulation capabilities, but proprietary or licensed implementations can restrict inspection and modification of the underlying propagation and signal-generation algorithms. AuRaSim instead provides an accessible and extensible research framework for automotive FMCW radar studies.

## III Preliminaries

*Fig. 1: Principal propagation mechanisms considered by the Path Solver: specular reflection, diffuse scattering, thin-slab transmission, and edge diffraction.*

### III-A FMCW Radar Signal Processing

An FMCW radar estimates target range and relative radial velocity from the frequency and phase evolution of the dechirped received signal. The complex transmit signal under the linear FMCW signal model [38] can be written as

$$ \ s_{\mathrm{tx}}(t)=\exp\left\{\jmath 2\pi\left(f_{c}t+\frac{\mu}{2}t^{2}\right)\right\},\qquad 0\leq t<T_{c}, $$

where $s_{\mathrm{tx}}(t)$ denotes the complex transmitted waveform, $t$ is the fast-time variable within one chirp, $f_{c}$ is the carrier frequency, $\mu$ is the linear frequency slope, and $T_{c}$ denotes the chirp duration. The imaginary unit is denoted by $\jmath$ .

For a point target at range $R$ moving with relative radial velocity $v$ , the round-trip propagation delay $\tau$ and Doppler frequency $\nu$ over one chirp are approximately

$$ \tau=\frac{2R}{c_{0}},\qquad\nu=\frac{2v}{\lambda_{0}}, $$

where $c_{0}$ is the speed of light, and $\lambda_{0}=c_{0}/f_{c}$ is the wavelength at the carrier frequency. Accordingly, the received signal can be modeled as

$$ s_{\mathrm{rx}}(t)=A\,s_{\mathrm{tx}}(t-\tau)e^{\jmath 2\pi\nu t}, $$

where $A$ denotes the complex path coefficient accounting for propagation loss, antenna responses, and electromagnetic interactions such as reflection and scattering. After dechirping and neglecting the quadratic delay term $-\mu\tau^{2}/2$ , which is negligible for short-range automotive radar when $\tau/T_{c}\ll 1$ [39], the corresponding intermediate-frequency (IF) signal is modeled as

$$ s_{\mathrm{IF}}(t)=A\exp\left\{\jmath 2\pi\left[\left(\mu\tau-\nu\right)t+f_{c}\tau\right]\right\}, $$

where the term $\mu\tau-\nu$ determines the beat frequency, whereas $f_{c}\tau$ represents the delay-dependent carrier phase.

After analog-to-digital conversion through ADC, the IF signal is sampled along the fast-time dimension within each chirp, while successive chirps form the slow-time dimension. The phase evolution in the fast-time signal mainly contains range-dependent beat-frequency information, whereas the phase progression across slow time encodes Doppler frequency. For multi-channel radar systems, the relative phase between the complex-valued IF signals across antenna channels additionally contains angular information. These dimensions jointly form the multi-channel ADC cube, which is formed by coherently summing the beat-signal contributions of all resolved propagation paths while preserving their relative phases across samples, chirps, and antenna channels. The corresponding path-to-ADC synthesis and the temporal approximation used in AuRaSim are described in detail in Sec. IV-E.

### III-B Sionna RT Path Solver

This subsection summarizes the Sionna RT propagation formulation relevant to AuRaSim, while further implementation details are provided in [15].

#### III-B1 Ray Sampling

Spherical Fibonacci lattice sampling has been adopted in previous works [19, 16] to initialize SBR rays. Compared with a uniform angular grid, directly sampling azimuth and polar angles with constant angular increments leads to nonuniform point density on the sphere, with excessive samples near the poles. Fibonacci sampling instead provides a deterministic and approximately equal-area distribution over the sphere with reduced clustering, allowing a given number of rays to cover the angular domain more efficiently.

For $N_{\mathrm{ray}}$ rays, the spherical Fibonacci angles are defined as

$$ \theta_{n}=\arccos\left(1-\frac{2n}{N_{\mathrm{ray}}-1}\right),\phi_{n}=2\pi\,\mathrm{frac}\left(\frac{n}{\phi_{g}}\right) $$

where $n=0,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{ray}}-1$ , $\phi_{g}=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$ denotes the golden ratio, and $\operatorname{frac}(x)=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$ denotes the fractional part of $x$ . The corresponding initial unit propagation direction of the $n$ -th ray is

$$ {\boldsymbol{k}}_{n}^{(0)}=\begin{bmatrix}\sin\theta_{n}\cos\phi_{n}\\
\sin\theta_{n}\sin\phi_{n}\\
\cos\theta_{n}\end{bmatrix}. $$

This distribution covers the complete sphere, such that each initial ray tube represents an approximately equal solid angle

$$ \Delta\Omega_{\mathrm{full}}\approx\frac{4\pi}{N_{\mathrm{ray}}}. $$

#### III-B2 SBR Candidate Generation

SBR traces rays launched from the transmitter through successive interactions with the scene geometry to identify candidate propagation paths. To avoid the exponential growth that would result from spawning all physically possible continuations at every intersection, at most one interaction type is sampled for each ray and path depth. At the $\ell$ -th propagation interaction, the selected type $\chi^{(\ell)}$ is drawn from the set $\mathcal{X}$ with probability $p_{\chi}$ as

$$ \mathcal{X}=\{\mathcal{R},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{D}\},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{{\chi^{(\ell)}}\in\mathcal{X}}p_{\chi^{(\ell)}}=1,\quad p_{\chi^{(\ell)}}\geq 0, $$

where specular reflection $\mathcal{R}$ , diffuse scattering $\mathcal{S}$ , and transmission $\mathcal{T}$ are importance-sampled from the material response and Fresnel coefficients, while diffraction $\mathcal{D}$ is assigned a separately specified sampling probability to ensure sufficient exploration of weak diffracted paths.

#### III-B3 Electromagnetic Propagation Mechanisms

The four interaction mechanisms considered by the Path Solver are illustrated in Fig. 1. They affect both the geometry of the propagation path and its complex electromagnetic field.

#### Specular Reflection

For a smooth surface with unit normal $\boldsymbol{n}$ , the outgoing ray direction follows the geometrical-optics reflection law

$$ {\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathrm{r}}={\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathrm{i}}-2\left({\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathrm{i}}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{n}\right)\boldsymbol{n}, $$

where ${\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathrm{i}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathrm{r}}$ denote the incident and reflected unit propagation directions. The reflected field is obtained by applying the polarization-dependent complex Fresnel response of the assigned radio material to the incident field.

#### Diffuse Scattering

Sionna RT models diffuse reflection using an effective-roughness formulation, where the scattering coefficient $S\in[0,1]$ determines the fraction $S^{2}$ of the total reflected power assigned to diffuse scattering, while the normalized scattering pattern $f_{\mathrm{s}}$ specifies its angular distribution over the outward hemisphere $\mathcal{H}^{+}$ ,

$$ \int_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}f_{\mathrm{s}}\left({\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathrm{i}},{\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathrm{s}}\right)\mathrm{d}\Omega=1. $$

Sionna RT provides several scattering patterns based on effective-roughness models [40]. The Lambertian model is used by default and distributes the scattered energy around the surface normal according to

$$ f_{\mathrm{L}}(\theta_{\mathrm{s}})=\frac{\cos\theta_{\mathrm{s}}}{\pi},\qquad\theta_{\mathrm{s}}\in[0,\pi/2], $$

where $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}$ denotes the angle between the scattering direction and the surface normal. The directive model instead concentrates the scattered field around the ideal specular-reflection direction, with its lobe width controlled by a directivity parameter. The backscattering model further introduces an additional lobe toward the incident direction, enabling enhanced return toward the source.

Unlike specular reflection, diffuse scattering distributes energy over a continuum of outgoing directions. Sionna RT handles this using next-event estimation, which explicitly tests the connection from each diffuse interaction point to the receiver. If the receiver is visible, the corresponding receiver-directed contribution is retained as a candidate path and weighted according to the scattering model. An outgoing direction is then sampled stochastically from the scattering distribution to continue the SBR trajectory and explore higher-order propagation paths, while the corresponding interaction-sampling and ray-tube solid-angle weights are applied during field evaluation to compensate for the stochastic sampling and properly normalize the resulting path contributions.

#### Transmission

Sionna RT models transmissive surfaces using a homogeneous thin-slab approximation. The effective slab transmission coefficient is expressed as

$$ T_{q}(\delta)=\frac{(1-r_{q}^{2})e^{-{\jmath}\psi}}{1-r_{q}^{2}e^{-\jmath 2\psi}},\qquad\psi=k_{0}\delta\sqrt{\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{r}-\sin^{2}\theta_{\mathrm{i}}}. $$

Here, $q$ indexes the two polarization components with respect to the plane of incidence, i.e., perpendicular ( $\perp$ ) and parallel ( $\parallel$ ), and $r_{q}$ denotes the corresponding single-interface Fresnel reflection coefficient. Moreover, $\delta$ is the effective material thickness, $k_{0}=2\pi/\lambda_{0}$ is the free-space wavenumber, and $\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{r}$ is the complex relative permittivity determined by the material permittivity and conductivity. The numerator accounts for transmission through the two slab interfaces and propagation through the slab, whereas the denominator captures the effect of internal multiple reflections.

#### Edge Diffraction

Geometrical optics alone cannot represent fields propagating around sharp edges into geometrical shadow regions. Sionna RT therefore models edge diffraction using the uniform theory of diffraction (UTD) [41]. For an edge with unit direction ${\boldsymbol{e}}$ , the incident and diffracted rays satisfy the Keller-cone condition

$$ {\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathrm{i}}^{\mathsf{T}}{\boldsymbol{e}}={\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathrm{d}}^{\mathsf{T}}{\boldsymbol{e}}=\cos\beta_{0}. $$

where $\beta_{0}$ denotes the angle between the incident ray and the diffracting edge. The UTD diffraction coefficient determines the complex amplitude and phase of the diffracted field as a function of wavelength, wedge geometry, incidence and observation directions, and the electromagnetic properties of the wedge faces. UTD transition functions provide a continuous field description across geometrical shadow boundaries, and only first-order diffraction is considered in Sionna RT.

#### III-B4 Image-Method Path Refinement

The SBR stage primarily identifies candidate interaction sequences rather than exact propagation paths between transmitter and receiver. While diffuse interactions can directly connect to a visible receiver through next-event estimation, randomly sampled specular, transmitted, or diffracted rays have essentially zero probability of intersecting a point receiver. Sionna RT therefore uses an image-method-based refinement to determine the exact interaction points of suitable candidate sequences such that they connect the transmitter and receiver and satisfy the corresponding propagation constraints.

For specular chains, the source is successively mirrored across the candidate reflection planes, so that the multi-bounce path can be solved as an equivalent straight-line connection to the receiver. The reflection points are subsequently obtained by tracing this connection back through the corresponding surfaces. Transmission events are included without angular deflection under the thin-slab approximation, while candidates containing first-order diffraction are handled in image space by additionally constraining the diffraction point to the corresponding wedge. Candidates whose refined interaction points lie outside the associated primitives or whose paths are occluded are discarded.

#### III-B5 Electromagnetic Field Calculation

After the geometric path has been validated, Sionna RT evaluates the complex electromagnetic field along the complete interaction sequence. Starting from the transmit antenna response, every interaction applies a complex polarization-dependent transfer matrix $\mathbf{T}_{p,\ell}$ corresponding to reflection, diffuse scattering, transmission, or diffraction. The receive antenna pattern is subsequently evaluated in the final arrival direction.

The complex path coefficient can be summarized as

$$ \displaystyle A_{p}=\underbrace{\frac{\lambda_{0}}{4\pi}G_{p}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{geometric spreading}\\
\text{and normalization}\end{subarray}}\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{rx}}^{\mathrm{H}}\left(-{\boldsymbol{k}}_{p}^{(L)}\right)}_{\text{receive antenna}}\;\underbrace{\left[\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbf{T}_{p,\ell}\right]}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{material and}\\
\text{EM interactions}\end{subarray}}\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{tx}}\left({\boldsymbol{k}}_{p}^{(0)}\right)}_{\text{transmit antenna}}, $$

where $\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{tx}}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{rx}}$ denote the complex transmit and receive antenna field responses, and $(\cdot)^{\mathrm{H}}$ denotes the Hermitian transpose. The interaction matrices $\mathbf{T}_{p,\ell}$ are applied in propagation order from the transmitter toward the receiver. The factor $G_{p}$ denotes the path-dependent geometric spreading factor, including the normalization required for stochastic ray sampling. For diffuse paths, $G_{p}$ additionally accounts for the interaction-sampling and ray-tube weights. For diffracted paths, the corresponding UTD spreading factor is used.

## IV Radar Simulation System

AuRaSim provides a complete automotive radar simulation chain for dynamic scenarios. Following the system overview in Sec. IV-A, antenna characteristics and waveform parameters are defined in Sec. IV-B. The Blender Scenario Builder (Sec. IV-C) constructs and updates the dynamic scene. The Path Solver (Sec. IV-D) resolves material- and motion-dependent propagation paths. Finally, the ADC Signal Synthesizer (Sec. IV-E) converts these paths into radar signals. This modular design preserves traceability throughout the simulation pipeline while allowing individual stages to be inspected and reused independently.

### IV-A System Overview

*Fig. 2: System overview of AuRaSim. A trajectory-driven dynamic digital twin and a configurable radar sensor are synchronized at each radar timestamp. The Path Solver produces an explicit path-level representation, which is subsequently converted into waveform-consistent multi-channel ADC samples and derived radar products.*

As illustrated in Fig. 2, AuRaSim maps a dynamic digital-twin scene and a configurable radar sensor to multi-channel radar ADC signals. The Radar Sensor Configuration defines the antenna layout, radiation patterns, waveform, and acquisition parameters, while the Blender Scenario Builder provides the time-varying scene geometry and motion state. For each radar frame, the Path Solver resolves the path set $\mathcal{P}=\{P_{p}\}$ , containing the complex coefficients, delays, Doppler frequencies, and propagation geometry required by the ADC Signal Synthesizer, which subsequently converts these paths into a complex multi-channel ADC cube according to the configured waveform and sampling scheme. Retaining $\mathcal{P}$ decouples the propagation stage from waveform-dependent ADC synthesis.

### IV-B Radar Sensor Configuration

AuRaSim provides a parameter-configurable radar sensor model that consists of three main components: MIMO setup, antenna radiation patterns, and waveform parameters.

#### IV-B1 MIMO Configuration

The antenna layout specifies the number and relative positions of the transmitters and receivers by $\boldsymbol{d}^{\mathrm{tx}}_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and $\boldsymbol{d}^{\mathrm{rx}}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , respectively. AuRaSim supports both explicit-array tracing, in which propagation is evaluated for individual transmit–receive positions, and a reference-array approximation, in which propagation is traced between the array reference positions and the responses of individual transmit–receive channels are reconstructed using element-dependent phase offsets derived from the departure and arrival directions. For time-division multiplexing (TDM)-MIMO, the transmit sequence is additionally retained to preserve the temporal relationship between virtual-array channels. The corresponding channel synthesis is described in Sec. IV-E.

#### IV-B2 Antenna Pattern

The antenna radiation pattern is represented by the direction-dependent complex field response $\boldsymbol{F}(\theta,\phi)$ , where $\theta$ and $\phi$ denote the polar and azimuth directions. Customized antenna patterns can be interpolated at the propagation directions required by the ray tracer. The resulting antenna responses are incorporated into the electromagnetic field calculation described in Sec. III-B5.

#### IV-B3 Waveform Parameters

Signals with different waveforms can be synthesized by specifying the corresponding transmit waveform and sampling scheme. In this work, we focus on automotive FMCW radar. The configurable waveform parameters include the carrier frequency $f_{c}$ , effective bandwidth $B$ , chirp slope $\mu$ , chirp and idle durations, ADC sampling frequency $f_{s}$ , number of ADC samples per chirp $N_{s}$ , and number of chirps per radar frame $N_{c}$ .

### IV-C Blender Scenario Builder

The Blender Scenario Builder constructs plausible dynamic driving scenes from trajectory-level descriptions and provides the downstream Path Solver with synchronized geometry and mesh motion state. Given object trajectories and semantic classes, corresponding 3D assets are retrieved from the asset library, placed into the scene, and animated according to their motion over time. We use Blender[14] as the digital-twin front end because it provides mature support for polygon meshes, asset management, rigid-body motion, skeletal animation, and evaluated deformable geometry.

#### IV-C1 Dynamic Scene Representation and Persistent Update

AuRaSim partitions the scene geometry into three categories,

$$ \mathcal{G}(t)=\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{stat}}\cup\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{rig}}(t)\cup\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{def}}(t), $$

where $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{stat}}$ denotes static infrastructure, $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{rig}}(t)$ rigid dynamic objects, and $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{def}}(t)$ articulated or deformable objects. Typical examples include roads and buildings, vehicles, and pedestrians, respectively.

Blender evaluates the complete animation state at each requested radar time $t_{k}$ . Scene semantics are used to select the corresponding mesh and animation configuration from the 3D asset library. Vehicle assets are animated using a Blender vehicle-rigging workflow such as Rigacar [42], allowing the vehicle body, steering, and wheel rotation to be synchronized with the trajectory. Articulated human meshes use skeletal animations, e.g., motion assets from Adobe Mixamo [43], adapted to the specified pedestrian trajectories. In this way, different parts of a dynamic object are not restricted to a single object-level velocity, allowing more plausible vehicle and pedestrian motion to be represented.

Repeatedly rebuilding and transferring the complete electromagnetic scene to GPU for every radar frame would introduce substantial computational overhead. To avoid this, AuRaSim introduces a persistent propagation-scene update strategy that treats static, rigid, and deformable geometry differently. Static geometry is instantiated once with simulation initialization, rigid objects are updated through their transformations, and deformable objects retain their triangle connectivity while only their evaluated vertex positions are updated.

#### IV-C2 Radio Material Assignment

The 3D asset library stores electromagnetic material information independently of the visual materials used for rendering. During scene construction, each mesh is assigned a radio material according to its semantic and physical properties. AuRaSim uses the radio-material representation provided by Sionna RT [15], including its built-in International Telecommunication Union (ITU) material models for common materials such as concrete, glass, wood, brick, metal and ground surfaces.

Each radio material specifies its electromagnetic properties, including permittivity, conductivity, material thickness, diffuse-scattering coefficient, cross-polarization coefficient, and scattering pattern. For the built-in ITU material models, the electromagnetic properties are frequency dependent and are evaluated at the configured radar frequency. The Path Solver subsequently uses these material properties for material-dependent propagation interactions.

*Fig. 3: The Path Solver pipeline of AuRaSim. Black components correspond to the Sionna RT $\mathtt{PathSolver}$ , while red components indicate the radar-oriented adaptations introduced in AuRaSim. AuRaSim restricts the initial ray distribution to the radar field of view, applies path filtering before field evaluation, provides local hit-point velocities for Doppler calculation, and exports an explicit path-level representation for subsequent radar signal synthesis.*

#### IV-C3 Vertex-Velocity Field

Sionna RT represents the motion of each dynamic scene object by a single velocity vector $\boldsymbol{v}(o)$ , which is shared by all propagation interactions occurring on that object [15]. While this representation is suitable for objects undergoing approximately uniform translational motion, it cannot capture spatially varying surface velocities caused by rotation, articulation or deformation.

For automotive radar simulation, such local motion is particularly relevant. Points on a rotating wheel exhibit different instantaneous velocities from the car body, while the limbs of an articulated pedestrian undergo additional motion relative to the pedestrian trajectory. To capture these effects, AuRaSim introduces a world-space vertex-velocity field for the dynamic scene geometry that can be queried at individual interactions.

For rigid objects, the velocity of vertex $i$ is obtained from the translational and rotational motion of the object,

$$ \boldsymbol{v}_{i}(t_{k})=\boldsymbol{v}_{o}(t_{k})+\boldsymbol{\omega}_{o}(t_{k})\times\left[\boldsymbol{x}_{i}(t_{k})-\boldsymbol{p}_{o}(t_{k})\right], $$

where $\boldsymbol{v}_{o}$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{o}$ denote the translational and angular velocities of the object, respectively, $\boldsymbol{p}_{o}$ is its world-space reference position, and $\boldsymbol{x}_{i}$ is the world-space vertex position. The angular velocity is estimated from temporally adjacent rigid transformations. This representation naturally captures local velocity variations caused by object rotation, such as the motion of vehicle wheels.

For articulated or deformable objects, the complete Blender animation stack is first evaluated, and the vertex velocity ${v}_{i}(t_{k})$ at an interior timestamp $t_{k}$ is estimated using a centered finite-difference approximation

$$ \boldsymbol{v}_{i}(t_{k})=\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_{i}(t_{k+1})-\boldsymbol{x}_{i}(t_{k-1})}{t_{k+1}-t_{k-1}}. $$

Since it is applied after rigid transformations, skeletal articulation, and mesh deformation have been evaluated by Blender, the resulting velocity implicitly contains both global motion and local deformation. One-sided differences are used at the temporal boundaries.

For a ray intersecting a triangle formed by vertices $i_{1}$ , $i_{2}$ , and $i_{3}$ , the local surface velocity is obtained by barycentric interpolation [44],

$$ \boldsymbol{v}_{h}=\sum_{q=1}^{3}\beta_{q}\boldsymbol{v}_{i_{q}},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{q=1}^{3}\beta_{q}=1,\ \beta_{q}\geq 0, $$

where $\beta_{q}$ denotes the barycentric coordinate associated with the $q$ -th triangle vertex.

To make this motion information directly accessible during propagation, Since Sionna RT is built on Mitsuba 3 [45], AuRaSim extends the corresponding Mitsuba mesh representation with a custom per-vertex velocity attribute. The world-space velocity field is transferred together with the updated mesh geometry, allowing the Path Solver to retrieve and interpolate the local velocity directly at each ray–surface interaction. The resulting hit-point velocity $\boldsymbol{v}_{h}^{(\ell)}$ of $\ell$ -th interaction point along a propagation path is subsequently used in the motion-aware Doppler formulation described in Sec. IV-D3.

### IV-D Path Solver

The AuRaSim Path Solver pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 3. At each timestamp, the current dynamic scene state is passed to the Path Solver, which combines SBR with image-method refinement to determine valid propagation paths and subsequently evaluates their complex electromagnetic fields. AuRaSim adapts the Sionna RT pipeline to automotive radar simulation by introducing radar-oriented ray sampling and filtering, hit-point-level motion information, and an explicit path representation for waveform-level signal synthesis.

#### IV-D1 FOV Ray Sampling

Building on the spherical Fibonacci sampling described in Sec. III-B1, AuRaSim restricts the initial ray distribution to the radar-relevant Field-Of-View (FOV). Instead of generating rays over the complete sphere and subsequently discarding those outside the radar field of view, AuRaSim directly maps the Fibonacci sequence into the admissible region $\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}$ . Let $\theta\in[\theta_{\min},\theta_{\max}]$ and $\phi\in[\phi_{\min},\phi_{\max}]$ denote the configured polar and azimuth ranges. The modified angles are

$$ \theta_{n}^{\prime}=\arccos\left[\cos\theta_{\mathrm{\min}}-\frac{n}{N_{\mathrm{ray}}-1}\left(\cos\theta_{\mathrm{\min}}-\cos\theta_{\mathrm{\max}}\right)\right], $$

and

$$ \phi_{n}^{\prime}=\phi_{\mathrm{\min}}+\left(\phi_{\mathrm{\max}}-\phi_{\mathrm{\min}}\right)\mathrm{frac}\left(\frac{n}{\phi_{g}}\right). $$

The initial ray directions are then obtained from (3) by replacing $\theta_{n}$ and $\phi_{n}$ with $\theta_{n}^{\prime}$ and $\phi_{n}^{\prime}$ , respectively. The nonlinear mapping of $\theta$ preserves approximately uniform solid-angle sampling within the restricted angular domain.

Because AuRaSim changes the sampling domain itself rather than applying a post-hoc angular filter, all $N_{\mathrm{ray}}$ samples remain available for the radar-relevant region. For the same number of launched rays, this increases the angular sampling density within the radar field of view, as illustrated in Fig. 4. Conversely, achieving the same in-FOV sampling density with full-sphere sampling would require substantially more rays and therefore higher ray-tracing cost.

As in Sec. III-B1, each launched ray represents a finite solid angle. Restricting the sampling domain therefore requires updating this per-ray solid-angle weight. For the rectangular angular region considered above, the corresponding solid-angle weight per launched ray is

$$ \Delta\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}=\frac{|\left(\phi_{\mathrm{\max}}-\phi_{\mathrm{\min}}\right)\left(\cos\theta_{\mathrm{\min}}-\cos\theta_{\mathrm{\max}}\right)|}{N_{\mathrm{ray}}}. $$

The propagation weights are therefore evaluated using $\Delta\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}$ , such that concentrating the ray samples within the radar field of view improves sampling efficiency without artificially changing the represented electromagnetic energy.

The proposed FOV-aware Fibonacci sampling concentrates the same number of rays directly within the radar field of view.*

#### IV-D2 Path Filtering

Before path refinement and electromagnetic field evaluation, AuRaSim applies a radar-specific filtering stage to discard propagation paths that cannot contribute to the radar observation. For each candidate path $p$ , the arrival direction and propagation distance are checked against the configured receive field of view and maximum distance threshold. The path is retained only if

$$ \mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{filter}}(p)=\mathbb{I}\left[-{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\mathrm{arr}}_{p}\in\Omega_{\mathrm{rx}}\right]\mathbb{I}\left[d_{p}\leq d_{\max}\right], $$

where ${\boldsymbol{k}}^{\mathrm{arr}}_{p}$ denotes the arrival direction of path $p$ , $\Omega_{\mathrm{rx}}$ is the admissible receive angular region, $d_{p}$ is the propagation length, and $d_{\max}$ is the configured maximum length. Paths that violate either condition are discarded to avoid unnecessary path refinement and field evaluation for SBR candidates outside the useful radar observation region.

#### IV-D3 Hit-Point Doppler

Sionna RT computes path Doppler by accumulating the velocity contributions of the objects intersected along the propagation path. In its standard mobility formulation, each scene object is associated with a single velocity vector $\boldsymbol{v}(o)$ , which is applied identically to all interaction points on that object [15]. This object-level approximation cannot represent the spatially varying motion of rotating, articulated, or deformable meshes.

AuRaSim replaces $\boldsymbol{v}(o)$ with the local hit-point velocity $\boldsymbol{v}_{h}^{(\ell)}$ at the $\ell$ -th interaction point, described in Sec. IV-C3. For a resolved propagation path $p$ containing $L$ interaction points and therefore $L+1$ propagation segments, the total first-order Doppler frequency $\nu_{p}$ is

$$ \nu_{p}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}}\left[\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{tx}}^{\mathsf{T}}{\boldsymbol{k}}_{p}^{(0)}-\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{rx}}^{\mathsf{T}}{\boldsymbol{k}}_{p}^{(L)}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{h}^{(\ell)}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\left({\boldsymbol{k}}_{p}^{(\ell)}-{\boldsymbol{k}}_{p}^{(\ell-1)}\right)\right]. $$

Here, $\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{tx}}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{rx}}$ denote the transmitter and receiver velocities, respectively, while ${\boldsymbol{k}}_{p}^{(\ell)}$ , $\ell=0,\ldots,L$ , denotes the unit propagation direction of the corresponding path segment. Thus, the index $\ell=0$ denotes the segment leaving the transmitter, while $\ell=L$ denotes the final segment arriving at the receiver. The first two terms account for transmitter and receiver motion, whereas each term in the summation represents the Doppler contribution of a moving interaction point through its velocity projected onto the change between the outgoing and incoming propagation directions. Replacing the object-level velocity with $\boldsymbol{v}_{h}^{(\ell)}$ therefore allows different locations on the same mesh to produce distinct Doppler shifts during waveform-level signal synthesis.

#### IV-D4 Path Representation

Each valid propagation path is exported as an explicit intermediate record

$$ P_{p}=\left\{A_{p},\,\tau_{p},\,\nu_{p},\,{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\mathrm{dep}}_{p},\,{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\mathrm{arr}}_{p},\,\mathbf{X}_{p}\right\}, $$

where $\tau_{p}$ denotes the propagation delay, ${\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{dep}}_{p}$ denotes the departure and arrival unit directions, and $\mathbf{X}_{p}$ contains the ordered interaction points along the path.

This path-level representation separates the computationally expensive propagation stage from waveform-dependent signal generation, allowing reuse for different waveform and acquisition configurations without repeating the ray-tracing computation and providing the input to the ADC Signal Synthesizer described in Sec. IV-E.

### IV-E ADC Signal Synthesizer

The ADC Signal Synthesizer converts the resolved propagation paths into complex sampled FMCW beat signals through coherent superposition. In contrast to adding received powers independently, coherent synthesis preserves the path phases and therefore captures constructive and destructive interference between multipath components.

#### IV-E1 MIMO Array Modeling

In explicit-array mode, propagation paths are evaluated for individual transmit–receive pairs. In synthetic-array mode, ray tracing is performed between the array reference positions, and the element-dependent phase differences are subsequently reconstructed from the path departure and arrival directions.

For path $p$ , the phase compensation factor for transmitter $u$ and receiver $r$ is

$$ c_{p,r,u}=\exp\left\{j\frac{2\pi}{\lambda_{0}}\left[\left({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\mathrm{dep}}_{p}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{d}^{\mathrm{tx}}_{u}-\left({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\mathrm{arr}}_{p}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{d}^{\mathrm{rx}}_{r}\right]\right\}. $$

The synthetic-array formulation assumes that the wavefront is approximately planar across the array aperture, such that the propagation path can be treated as common to all antenna elements and the element-dependent path-length differences can be represented by phase shifts. This approximation is valid when the array aperture is sufficiently small relative to the propagation distance. When near-field effects or wavefront curvature become significant, explicit transmit–receive tracing can instead be used at increased computational cost.

#### IV-E2 Coherent Multipath Synthesis

Following the FMCW signal model introduced in (1), the resolved propagation paths are synthesized coherently for each receive antenna. For receive antenna $r$ , the sampled ADC signal $s_{r}[m,n]$ at chirp index $m$ and fast-time sample index $n$ is obtained by coherently summing all resolved propagation paths,

$$ \begin{split}s_{r}[m,n]=\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}&\underbrace{A_{p}}_{\text{path field}}\underbrace{c_{p,r,u(m)}}_{\text{MIMO}}\underbrace{e^{\jmath 2\pi f_{c}\tau_{p}}}_{\text{carrier phase}}\\
&\cdot\underbrace{e^{\jmath 2\pi(\mu\tau_{p}-\nu_{p})nT_{s}}}_{\text{fast time}}\underbrace{e^{-\jmath 2\pi\nu_{p}mT_{r}}}_{\text{slow time}}.\end{split} $$

Here, $T_{s}$ and $T_{r}$ denote the ADC sampling interval and chirp repetition interval, respectively. For explicit-array simulation, the channel-specific path coefficient $c_{p,r,u(m)}$ is not required.

By default, the path geometry is evaluated at a reference timestamp for each radar frame and is assumed to remain approximately unchanged during the corresponding coherent processing interval. Within the frame, dynamic objects and sensors are assumed to follow locally constant velocities, while their intra-frame motion is represented through the Doppler-induced phase progression across chirps. However, the local velocities are updated between successive frames according to the animated scene, allowing time-varying micro-Doppler signatures from articulated objects to be simulated. This frame-level path evaluation substantially reduces the computational cost while preserving coherent slow-time motion effects. AuRaSim additionally supports chirp-level simulation, in which the scene geometry and propagation paths are computed for individual chirps, at the cost of increased ray-tracing time.

## V Experiments

### V-A Data Preparation

#### V-A1 Dataset

The experiments are conducted on the dataset introduced by Gao et al. [46], which provides synchronized real radar measurements and RGB images for reconstructing and validating corresponding digital-twin scenarios. The full dataset contains approximately 19,800 synchronized raw radar frames and RGB images collected in campus, road, and parking-lot environments. Three common road-user categories are considered in this work: pedestrians, cyclists and cars.

#### V-A2 Digital-Twin Reconstruction

For signal-level evaluation, representative sequences from the dataset are reconstructed as corresponding digital-twin scenarios. The static environment is manually created and aligned with the radar coordinate system. Dynamic objects are detected from the synchronized RGB images using the WildDet3D [47], followed by temporal association, tracking, and trajectory smoothing. The corresponding 3D assets are instantiated and animated according to the recovered trajectories, resulting in temporally synchronized digital-twin scenes as described in Sec. IV-C. AuRaSim is then applied to these reconstructed scenes, and the simulated radar data are compared with the corresponding measured radar data. These scenes are subsequently used for the real-to-sim validation and ablation studies presented in the following sections.

#### V-A3 Parameters

The measurements were acquired using a Texas Instruments AWR1843 radar operating at 77 GHz. The radar configuration is summarized in Table I. The same reconstructed scene geometry, antenna layout, antenna pattern, waveform, and sampling configuration are reproduced in AuRaSim and RadarSimPy [37] which is used as a physics-based baseline for comparison with AuRaSim. Both configurations are chosen to closely match the measurement setup. The ray-tracing backend of RadarSimPy controls spatial sampling through a ray-density parameter rather than an explicit launched-ray count. For the baseline experiments with RadarSimPy, the density is set to $\rho_{\mathrm{ray}}=\mathrm{0.1}$ rays per wavelength squared, with a maximum reflection order of 3 and diffuse scattering enabled. This value was selected as the highest stable setting for the reconstructed scenes used in our experiments, as higher ray densities consistently resulted in GPU execution failures on our test system. ### V-B Evaluation Metrics

For all signal-level comparisons, the measured and simulated ADC data are processed using the same range–Doppler pipeline. The resulting RD power maps are independently normalized, converted to logarithmic scale, and clipped to a range of $-60$ dB to $0$ dB. The normalized dB values are subsequently mapped to $[0,1]$ for quantitative evaluation. Let $\widetilde{M}^{\mathrm{real}}_{i,j}$ and $\widetilde{M}^{\mathrm{sim}}_{i,j}$ denote the normalized log-power values of the measured and simulated RD maps at range bin $i$ and Doppler bin $j$ , respectively. The root-mean-square error (RMSE) is

$$ \mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N_{R}N_{D}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{R}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{D}}\left(\widetilde{M}^{\mathrm{real}}_{i,j}-\widetilde{M}^{\mathrm{sim}}_{i,j}\right)^{2}}, $$

and the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) is

$$ \mathrm{PSNR}=20\log_{10}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{RMSE}}\right). $$

Here, $N_{R}$ and $N_{D}$ denote the numbers of range and Doppler bins, respectively. Lower RMSE and higher PSNR indicate closer agreement with the measured radar response.

#### V-E1 Effect of the Number of Rays

Experiments E1–E4 isolate the influence of the number of launched rays while keeping the remaining components unchanged. Increasing the ray count from 0.1 to 10 million consistently improves the agreement with the measured range–Doppler map, increasing the PSNR from 16.81 dB to 19.40 dB. At the same time, the runtime increases from 0.672 s/frame to 0.838 s/frame.

The qualitative results in Fig. 7(b)–(e) show the same tendency. At low sampling densities, only the dominant propagation contributions are recovered, and parts of the target response remain weak or incomplete. Increasing the number of rays resolves additional contributions and progressively recovers the target structure. Once the dominant geometric interactions of this scene are sufficiently sampled, however, the additional improvement becomes smaller while the ray-tracing cost continues to increase. The results indicate that the 5–10 million range already provides a dense representation for this particular scene.

#### V-E2 Effect of FOV Ray Sampling

Experiments E4 and E5 provide the direct ablation of the proposed FOV-aware sampling strategy at an identical budget of 10 million launched rays. Mapping the samples directly into the radar-relevant angular region increases the PSNR from 18.59 to 19.40 dB and slightly reduces the runtime from 0.859 to 0.838 s/frame. The difference arises because full-sphere sampling allocates a substantial fraction of the rays to directions outside the configured radar FOV.

For the full-sphere sampling, approximately half of the generated rays fall into the configured FOV used in this experiment. Consequently, E5 with 10 million full-sphere rays can also be compared with E3 using 5 million FOV-restricted rays as an approximate effective-sampling-density comparison. Despite using only half as many launched rays, E3 achieves a similar 18.71 dB compared with 18.59 dB for E5, while reducing the runtime from 0.859 to 0.774 s/frame, corresponding to a reduction of approximately 0.085 s, or 9.9%. This result demonstrates that concentrating the ray budget within the relevant angular region improves the efficiency of propagation sampling without increasing the total ray count.

#### V-E3 Effect of Path Filtering

Experiments E4 and E6 isolate the effect of the path-filtering stage. Removing the filter reduces the PSNR substantially from 19.40 to 15.46 dB, while the runtime decreases slightly from 0.838 to 0.826 s/frame. This indicates that path filtering improves the simulation quality with a small computational cost. Otherwise, additional responses from paths outside the configured radar observation region, particularly around zero Doppler, reduce the relative contrast of the target responses.

#### V-E4 Effect of Doppler Modeling

Finally, Experiments E4 and E7 evaluate the proposed local velocity-field formulation while keeping the ray count, FOV sampling, and path filtering unchanged. E7 uses the conventional object-level velocity representation, whereas E4 evaluates the Doppler contribution using the local hit-point velocity described in Sec. IV-D3. The proposed model improves the from 17.52 to 19.40 dB, while the measured runtime remains essentially unchanged at 0.837 and 0.838 s/frame, respectively.

The difference is particularly visible in the wheel-related region highlighted by the red boxes in Fig. 7. With the conventional object-level Doppler formulation in Fig. 7(h), the vehicle body remains visible because its translational motion is still represented. However, the additional Doppler spread associated with the rotating wheel is substantially weaker because all interaction points on the vehicle share the same object-level velocity. In contrast, the proposed hit-point formulation assigns spatially varying velocities to individual surface interaction points, resulting in a more realistic wheel-induced micro-Doppler distribution that better agrees with the measured radar response in Fig. 7(i).

## VI Conclusion

This paper presented AuRaSim, an end-to-end automotive FMCW radar simulation framework that connects dynamic digital-twin scenes, configurable MIMO radar sensors, physics-based propagation, and waveform-level signal synthesis within a common and traceable pipeline. Building on Blender and Sionna RT, AuRaSim supports static, rigid, and deformable scene geometry, configurable antenna patterns and radio materials, path-resolved electromagnetic propagation, motion-aware Doppler modeling and coherent multi-channel ADC generation. We evaluated the simulator using digital twins reconstructed from real 77-GHz automotive radar measurement scenarios. Quantitative comparison between simulated and measured range–Doppler maps yielded an average RMSE of $0.147$ and an average of $16.93$ dB across the evaluated sequences. These results indicate that AuRaSim can reproduce the dominant range–Doppler response structures observed in real measurements while retaining a physically interpretable scene-to-signal mapping.

However, the fidelity of physics-based simulation remains affected by the accuracy of electromagnetic material parameters. Sensor-specific effects such as noise, interference, phase noise, calibration errors, and adverse-weather phenomena are not explicitly modeled in the current framework. In addition, high-order multipath and dense dynamic scenes remain computationally demanding despite the proposed optimizations.

Future work will focus on measurement-driven calibration of material and sensor parameters, more complete modeling of environmental effects, and further acceleration of ray tracing and ADC synthesis. AuRaSim also provides a basis for differentiable inverse radar rendering, physics-guided Sim2Real transfer, and large-scale synthetic-data generation for downstream automotive radar perception.
